name: Hedonic Adaptation / Impact Bias
description: People adapt faster than expected to positive and negative experiences, and they also mispredict how intense or lasting those feelings will be. New features, rewards, or setbacks rarely feel as transformative for as long as teams or users expect.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to launch planning, delight features, gamification, subscription retention, roadmap prioritization, and long-term UX strategy: short-term 'wow' often fades faster than product teams predict -- the same adaptation mechanism behind Kahneman & Deaton's well-known finding that day-to-day happiness stops tracking additional income once basic needs are met (roughly \$75,000/year in their 2010 US sample), a real large-scale demonstration of the same effect outside product design entirely.
myth_risk_note: Update 2026-09-02: raised from moderate to high. Beyond Diener et al.'s (2006) theoretical critique that the hedonic-treadmill model oversimplifies (differential set points, changeable set points, independent well-being components), the specific founding anecdote this entry's design-practice shorthand is built on -- lottery winners failing to be happier than controls -- is now directly empirically disputed: Kim & Oswald (2020) show that correcting for a real measurement bias in the original small-sample study reverses the classic null finding entirely. The popular 'hedonic adaptation swallows windfall gains, so don't bother chasing big wins' framing rests on a specific historical result that a larger, corrected dataset now contradicts.
prevalence_note: Common in product-strategy, gamification, and long-term UX discussions about novelty decay and sustaining delight; 'hedonic adaptation' is now a recognizable design-pattern/glossary term, while 'impact bias' is somewhat more research-facing.

findings.description: In a small comparison of 22 major lottery winners, 29 paraplegic/quadriplegic accident victims, and controls, lottery winners were not significantly happier than controls and rated significantly less pleasure from ordinary daily events than controls did; accident victims' happiness, while lower than controls', did not differ from controls as dramatically as the severity of their circumstances might predict — early evidence interpreted as adaptation of subjective well-being back toward a baseline level following major positive or negative life events.
findings.source_title: Lottery Winners and Accident Victims: Is Happiness Relative?
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

findings.description: People systematically mispredict their future emotional reactions to events, showing an 'impact bias' that overestimates both the intensity and duration of the emotional reaction — driven in part by focalism (underweighting how much other, unrelated events will also shape future feelings) and by a failure to anticipate how quickly they will psychologically make sense of and cope with what happens, especially after negative events.
findings.source_title: Affective Forecasting: Knowing What to Want

applications.title: Kahneman & Deaton's income study: happiness plateaus around $75,000/year
applications.description: In a 2010 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton analyzed data from nearly half a million randomly selected US residents, measuring day-to-day emotional well-being (joy, stress, sadness, anger, affection) against household income. They found that low income is associated with lower emotional well-being, but beyond an average of about $75,000 per year, additional income showed no further association with day-to-day happiness, enjoyment, sadness, or stress -- a real, large-scale demonstration of hedonic adaptation to rising material circumstances.
applications.industry_context: income and well-being research / public policy
applications.ethical_note: This documents a real, large-scale, peer-reviewed finding about the limits of material circumstances on daily emotional well-being, not a persuasion or product-design case -- there is no party attempting to influence behavior here, only a real, well-corroborated empirical boundary on how much rising income continues to move day-to-day happiness.
